unit.title: The Soft Game
unit.summary: Why dinking; cross-court vs straight; attackable balls; reset; pop-ups; hands battle; speed-up.

lessons.title: Why we dink
lessons.objective: Explain why patience is a weapon.

payload.prompt: Why do pros spend so much time dinking instead of hitting hard?

options.text: Patience and control win more points than power at the net.
Hard shots are illegal at the net.
Dinking is easier than attacking.
The kitchen rule makes power useless.

explanation.correct: Patience is the foundation. A soft dink rally controls the point; the first person to pop the ball up loses.
explanation.incorrect: Power matters, but soft game wins points. Whoever makes a ball sit up first gives the other side an attack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Patience beats power at the net.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We spent like ten minutes just dinking back and forth. Felt slow.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's the game. Soft dinking is how pros win points.
Yeah, you should have just attacked it.
Pickleball is kind of boring then.
Why didn't you speed it up?

payload.translation: A long dink rally is not boring; it's a chess match where patience wins.

followUps.line: A ten-minute dink rally means you both have great control. That's pro-level skill.
followUps.why: Reframes the rally as a high-skill battle, not a waste.

followUps.line: Whoever pops it up first gives the other side an easy attack. So patience is the strategy.
followUps.why: Practical explanation of why dinking works.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Dink rallies are the heart of pickleball, not a flaw.

payload.prompt: Match each soft-game concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Slow-paced rallies of soft dinks near the kitchen, prioritizing patience and control over power.
A soft shot that lands in the opponent's kitchen; the foundation of the soft game.
The strategy of keeping the ball low and soft until an attackable opportunity appears.

distractorDefinitions: A hard, fast shot meant to end the rally
The area where you cannot stand

explanation.summary: The soft game is all about patience: dinking softly, waiting for a mistake, and attacking only when the ball sits up.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft game means patience, not power.

payload.prompt: Your opponent pops one up just above net height. Do you attack it?

scene.alt: Kitchen dink rally scenario: soft ball floats up slightly above net.

choices.label: No, dink it back into the kitchen

explanation.correct: Yes. A ball above net height is attackable. That's when the soft game ends and you finish the point.
explanation.incorrect: If the ball is high enough, attack it. The soft game is setting up that moment, not avoiding it.
explanation.sayThisLine: High ball = attack. Low ball = dink. Know the difference.

payload.prompt: Complete the soft-game strategy.
payload.template: In the soft game, {{strategy}} is the weapon. You {{when-attack}} until the ball sits up, then {{what-do}}.

explanation.correct: Soft game is patience: dink low and soft until your opponent pops one up, then attack.
explanation.incorrect: Patience is the soft-game strategy. Dink until the opponent makes a mistake, then finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: Patience, dink, attack. That's the rhythm.

lessons.title: Cross-court and straight
lessons.objective: Read dink patterns and where they go.

payload.prompt: Tap where a cross-court dink from the left kitchen lands.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of a pickleball court with kitchen zones and service boxes marked.

explanation.correct: Cross-court means opposite diagonal kitchen. A cross-court dink from the left lands in the right kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: Straight dinks go parallel down the line, not across the court diagonally.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cross-court is diagonal; straight is parallel.

payload.prompt: You notice your opponent keeps dinking cross-court to the same spot. What is the opportunity?

situation.narrative: Your opponent is in a pattern of cross-court dinks to the right side of the kitchen.

facts.label: Opportunity
facts.value: Dink straight or angle to catch them out of position

options.label: Dink straight to the left kitchen, making them run across
options.consequence: Correct. Breaking a pattern with a straight dink or angle pulls them out of position and creates an opening.

options.label: Keep dinking cross-court back to the same spot
options.consequence: You're playing their game. Break the pattern.
considerations: Patterns are there to be broken
The soft game includes court movement

payload.expertNote: The soft game is partly about pattern-breaking. If you notice a rhythm, change it.

payload.prompt: What does cross-court mean in dinking?

options.text: Diagonal to the opposite kitchen
Along the same sideline
A hard, angled shot
Over the net at a steep angle

explanation.correct: Cross-court means diagonal to the opposite kitchen (left to right or right to left).
explanation.incorrect: Cross-court is diagonal. Straight dinks stay parallel along the sideline.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cross-court: diagonal. Straight: along the line.

payload.prompt: Complete the dink strategy.
payload.template: Vary your dink placement {{frequency}}, using {{patterns}} to tire opponents and create pop-ups.

explanation.correct: Vary placement: cross-court, straight, angled, deep, shallow. Keep them moving and tired.
explanation.incorrect: Dink patterns (cross-court, straight, angled) force movement and create openings.
explanation.sayThisLine: Vary placement: cross-court, straight, angle.

payload.prompt: Match each dink placement to its description.

pairs.definition: A soft dink hit diagonally to the opposite kitchen.
A soft dink hit parallel along the sideline into the same kitchen.
A dink hit at a sharp angle, pulling an opponent off the sideline.

distractorDefinitions: A serve that lands in the kitchen

explanation.summary: Cross-court is diagonal, straight is parallel, angled is sharp. Mixing them keeps opponents moving.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cross-court, straight, angle: three placement weapons.

lessons.title: The attackable ball
lessons.objective: Spot a ball high enough to attack.

payload.prompt: Your opponent's dink is still descending and will land below net height. Do you attack it?

scene.alt: Dink scenario: ball descending, not at net height.

explanation.correct: No, reset it. An attackable ball is high enough to hit down at. A descending dink needs a soft reset.
explanation.incorrect: You can only attack if the ball is above net height when you hit it. Low balls get reset, not attacked.
explanation.sayThisLine: High ball = attack. Low ball = reset.

payload.prompt: The dink floats up to net height as it comes toward you. Can you attack it?

situation.narrative: A soft dink is coming at you, floating at net height right at the bounce zone.

options.label: Yes, attack a ball at net height
options.consequence: Correct. If it's at or above net height, you can hit down at it. That's attackable.
considerations: Below net height needs a reset

options.label: No, reset it to be safe
options.consequence: Safe, but you missed an attack. Net-height balls are at the edge of attackable.
considerations: But attacking is the right read

payload.expertNote: An attackable ball is one at or above net height when you hit it. That's your signal to finish.

payload.prompt: Match the ball situation to the right call.

pairs.definition: A ball high enough (at or above net height) that you can hit down at it aggressively.
A low ball (below net height) that requires a soft, absorbing touch.
A soft ball floating high, creating an easy attack for the opponent.

explanation.summary: Attackable = high enough to hit down at. Reset = low and soft. Pop-up = your mistake, opponent's opportunity.
explanation.sayThisLine: High ball = attack. Low ball = reset. Floater = opponent wins.

payload.prompt: What height makes a dink attackable?

options.text: At or above net height when you hit it
Any ball hit by an opponent
Only balls hit hard
Balls that land in the kitchen

explanation.correct: A ball is attackable when it reaches net height or higher. That's when you can hit down at it.
explanation.incorrect: Attackable means you can hit down at it. Low balls get reset, not attacked.
explanation.sayThisLine: Attackable: at or above net height.

lessons.title: Reset
lessons.objective: Explain the reset as a defensive soft shot.

payload.prompt: Your opponent hits a hard ball at your feet in the kitchen. You don't have time to set up an attack. What do you do?

situation.narrative: A hard drive is coming at you low and fast at the net.

facts.label: Time
facts.value: Not much for a full swing

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: Stay in the rally, neutralize the ball

options.label: Reset it: a soft, defensive shot that lands in the kitchen
options.consequence: Correct. A reset absorbs the pace and lands soft. It neutralizes the attack and keeps you alive.
considerations: It buys you time and position
Soft play wins the dink game back

options.label: Counter with a hard ball of your own
options.consequence: Risky. A hard counter when you're out of position usually goes out or sits up.

payload.expertNote: Reset is one of the most important soft-game shots. It neutralizes fast balls and returns you to the dink rhythm.

payload.prompt: When should you use a reset?

options.text: When a fast ball comes at you below net height and you need to neutralize it
Every time you dink
Only when serving
To counter an opponent's reset

explanation.correct: A reset is a defensive shot used when a fast ball comes at you low. It lands soft in the kitchen and neutralizes the attack.
explanation.incorrect: Reset is a defensive tool for fast balls below net height. It keeps you in the rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: Reset: soft defense against fast balls.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: They hit that hard at me and I just softly reset it. Then they hit it hard again and we went back and forth.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's a hands battle. Fast volleys at the net where both players are attacking and resetting.
You should have smashed it.
That sounds chaotic.
You should have given up.

payload.translation: Fast volley exchanges where both players attack and reset happen at the net and are called hands battles.

followUps.line: That back-and-forth is called a hands battle. Reflexes and compact swings win those.
followUps.why: Names the exchange and explains the skill.

followUps.line: Reset is a key tool in those exchanges. It buys you time to react.
followUps.why: Shows how reset fits into the bigger picture.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Reset is not a weakness; it's a core soft-game tool.

payload.prompt: A hard drive at your feet. Reset it soft into the kitchen instead of countering. Right call?

scene.alt: Scenario: hard fast ball coming low at the net.

choices.label: Yes, reset is the right call

explanation.correct: Yes. A reset neutralizes a fast ball and keeps you in the rally. It's smart defense.
explanation.incorrect: A reset when you're under pressure is exactly right. It absorbs pace and returns you to soft play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hard ball at your feet? Reset it soft into the kitchen.

payload.prompt: Complete the reset definition.
payload.template: A reset is a {{type}} shot that {{what-it-does}} a fast ball and lands {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Reset: a soft shot that absorbs pace and lands in the kitchen. It's defensive and keeps the rally alive.
explanation.incorrect: A reset is soft and absorbing, landing gently in the kitchen to neutralize fast balls.
explanation.sayThisLine: Reset: soft, absorbing, kitchen.

lessons.title: Pop-ups and counters
lessons.objective: Know why a pop-up loses the point and what a counter is.

payload.prompt: You hit a soft dink but it sits up just above the net. Did you just make a pop-up?

scene.alt: Scenario: dink sits up above net height.

explanation.correct: Yes, a pop-up is a soft ball that floats high, giving the opponent an easy attack.
explanation.incorrect: If your dink floats too high, that's a pop-up, and the opponent will attack it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pop-up: your mistake. Opponent's attack.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I popped it up and they smashed it for a winner. My fault.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's the game. Keep your dinks low; a pop-up is an easy attack.
You should have hit it harder.
They cheated with that smash.
Pickleball is unfair.

payload.translation: A pop-up is a dink that floats too high, and it gives the opponent an easy attack. It's a mistake that costs the point.

followUps.line: Pop it up and they smash. Low dink and they can't attack. So keep it low.
Everyone pops one up sometimes. The pros' pop-ups are rare because they have great touch.
followUps.why: Normalizes the mistake while showing the mastery goal.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Pop-ups happen. Keeping dinks low is a core soft-game skill.

payload.prompt: What is a pop-up?

options.text: A soft dink that floats too high, giving the opponent an easy attack
A serve that bounces high
Any ball hit high in the air
A fast volley at the net

explanation.correct: A pop-up is a dink that floats too high. The opponent attacks it and usually wins the point.
explanation.incorrect: Pop-up = dink floated too high. Keep dinks low and tight to avoid them.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pop-up: dink too high. Opponent smashes.

payload.prompt: Complete the pop-up and counter definition.
payload.template: A pop-up is {{what}}, while a counter-attack is {{type}} exchange {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Pop-up: dink floated high. Counter: fast exchange at the net where both players attack and defend.
explanation.incorrect: Pop-up is your mistake; counter-attack is a rally of fast volleys where opponents trade pace.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pop-up: mistake. Counter: fast battle.

payload.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

pairs.definition: A soft ball that floats up high, creating an easy attack for the opponent.
A fast exchange of volleys at the net where both players trade aggressive shots.
A dink that sits up or goes out, breaking the soft-game rhythm.

distractorDefinitions: A serve that lands in the kitchen
A ball hit from the baseline

explanation.summary: Pop-up is when you make a dink float high (your mistake). Counter-attack is a fast volley exchange.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pop-up = your mistake. Counter = fast battle.

lessons.title: The hands battle
lessons.objective: Understand the fast volley exchange at the line.

payload.prompt: Tap the beat as the volley exchange speeds up: tap as each shot lands.

explanation.correct: A hands battle is fast: both players volleying quick shots at the net, each trying to hit the other's shot softly or aggressively.
explanation.incorrect: Hands-battle timing is tight and fast. React quickly; compact swings matter more than power.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hands battle: fast, at the net, reflexes win.

payload.prompt: Match each volley term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A fast exchange of volleys at the kitchen line, often decided by reflexes and compact swings.
A compact, absorbing volley that returns a fast ball softly into the kitchen.
Hitting the ball before it bounces, usually at the net.

explanation.summary: Hands battle is the fast exchange. Block is a soft absorbing volley. Volley is any unbounced hit.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hands battle: fast volleys. Block: soft absorb.

payload.prompt: You and your opponent exchange three quick volleys at the net in rapid succession. Is this a hands battle?

scene.alt: Scenario: fast volley exchange at the kitchen line.

explanation.correct: Yes, a hands battle is a fast exchange of volleys at the net. Reflexes and compact swings matter.
explanation.incorrect: A fast volley exchange is a hands battle. It's different from the slow dink rhythm.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fast volleying at the net = hands battle.

payload.prompt: Complete the hands-battle strategy.
payload.template: In a hands battle, {{skill}} wins over power. A {{shot}} is your best tool to neutralize fast balls.

explanation.correct: Hands battle: reflexes and compact swings. Block is the key tool; it absorbs pace softly.
explanation.incorrect: Hands battle is won by quick reactions and the block. Power is not the answer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hands battle: reflexes and blocks.

payload.prompt: In a fast hands battle at the net, should you swing hard and aggressive?

situation.narrative: Fast volley exchange at the kitchen line, both players volleying quick shots.

facts.label: Your swing
facts.value: Limited room for a big swing

options.label: Keep it compact and block; reflexes win
options.consequence: Correct. In a hands battle, compact swings and absorbing blocks work better than power.
considerations: No room for a big swing

options.label: Go for a hard, aggressive swing
options.consequence: Risky. Hands battles are won by quick reactions, not power. You'll likely miss or pop it up.
considerations: Not enough space for a full swing
Fast hands work better than power
Aggressive swings miss at the net

payload.expertNote: Hands battles are won by reflexes and compact swings, not power. Block and counter-block.

lessons.title: When to speed up
lessons.objective: Decide when a speed-up is smart.

payload.prompt: You're in a long dink rally and notice your opponent is getting tired. Should you speed up?

situation.narrative: Soft dink rally has lasted 20+ shots. Your opponent looks fatigued.

options.label: Speed up and hit an aggressive shot to end the rally
options.consequence: Correct. After a long dink rally, when the opponent is tired, a speed-up can finish the point.
considerations: Timing matters: only when they're vulnerable

options.label: Keep dinking to make sure they break first
options.consequence: Safe, but you're missing the opportunity. A timely speed-up ends it now.
considerations: The tired opponent is your window
Know when to switch from soft to fast

payload.expertNote: Speed-up is the punctuation mark on a long dink rally. Use it when you sense fatigue or vulnerability.

payload.prompt: Tap the kitchen area where a well-timed speed-up should land.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of the court with kitchens and court zones marked.

explanation.correct: A speed-up is most effective when it lands hard and low in the opponent's kitchen, giving them little time to react.
explanation.incorrect: A speed-up from the back of the court is easier but less effective; the kitchen target is harder but more rewarding.
explanation.sayThisLine: Speed-up: hard into the kitchen.

payload.prompt: When is the best time to speed up during a soft-game rally?

options.text: When the opponent is tired or the ball sits up high enough to attack
Every other shot
After the first dink
Only in the final game of a match

explanation.correct: Speed up when you spot fatigue or an attackable ball. That's when it's most effective and least risky.
explanation.incorrect: Speed-up is a tactical tool, not random. Use it when you see an opening (fatigue, high ball).
explanation.sayThisLine: Speed-up: when they're tired or the ball is high.

payload.prompt: You're in the middle of a soft dink rally, the ball is low, and your opponent looks fresh. Do you speed up?

scene.alt: Scenario: low dink, early in rally, opponent ready.

explanation.correct: No, wait. Speed up when the opponent is tired or the ball is high. A premature speed-up is risky.
explanation.incorrect: Speed-up is tactical. Early in a rally when they're fresh, keep dinking and wait for your moment.
explanation.sayThisLine: Speed-up when they're tired, not when they're fresh.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I was dinking for a while and then I sped up and won the point. It felt perfect.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's the soft game! Dink until you see your opening, then speed up and finish.
You should speed up every time.
That was lucky.
Speed is the only thing that wins.

payload.translation: Timing a speed-up after a dink rally, when the opponent is tired or vulnerable, is smart strategy.

followUps.line: That's the rhythm: dink to set up, then speed up to finish. Perfect timing.
Recognizing the right moment to switch from soft to fast is the mark of a good player.
followUps.why: Shows it's a skill she's building.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Speed-up is the punctuation at the end of a dink rally, not the whole sentence.

payload.prompt: Which best describes a dink war?

options.text: A long soft-game rally where both sides are dinking patiently, trying to make the opponent pop one up
An argument over the rules
A series of hard shots back and forth
A game where only one player dinks

explanation.correct: A dink war is a patient rally of soft shots where both sides are in control, waiting for the mistake.
explanation.incorrect: Dink war is a strategic soft-game rally, not a conflict or a power exchange.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dink war: patient, soft, whoever pops first loses.

payload.title: After a dink-war rally
payload.setting: You and Sam are talking after an intense dink rally.

exchanges.theirMessage: That dink war was insane. We must have gone back and forth for like thirty shots.

replies.text: Thirty shots of dinking! Both of you had great control. Who finally popped one up?
replies.theirResponse: They did. Then I smashed it for the winner.
replies.coachNote: You valued the soft-game skill and asked who broke first.

replies.theirResponse: Yeah, it was exhausting but fun.
replies.coachNote: Neutral. Follow up with curiosity about the strategy.
Don't dismiss the soft game. It's chess at the net.

exchanges.theirMessage: Yeah, I kept dinking cross-court to tire them out.

replies.text: Good strategy, cross-court makes them move. Did they try to break the pattern?
replies.theirResponse: Eventually, yes. They went straight and almost got me.
replies.coachNote: You knew the strategy and asked about tactics.
Safe but ask about her decisions next time.

replies.text: Why didn't you just speed up from the start?
replies.coachNote: Speed-up is for the right moment, not the start.

payload.closingNote: A dink war is a test of patience and placement. The player with better control and strategy wins.

payload.prompt: Your opponent dinks to the same spot each time. Should you break the pattern or wait?

situation.narrative: Your opponent is in a predictable dink pattern.

facts.label: Opponent pattern
facts.value: Straight dinks to the same spot

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: Ready and expecting the straight shot

facts.label: Opening
facts.value: Can hit cross-court or angle to the other side

facts.label: Strategy
facts.value: Break the pattern or stay patient

options.label: Hit cross-court to the open side, pulling them out of position
options.consequence: Correct. Breaking a pattern forces movement and creates openings for a pop-up or winner.

options.label: Keep playing to the same spot and wait for them to change
options.consequence: Safe, but you're not using the information. Breaking the pattern is more efficient.
considerations: Force mistakes, don't wait for them

payload.expertNote: The soft game includes pattern recognition and pattern-breaking. If you see a rhythm, change it.

payload.prompt: Complete the dink-war strategy.
payload.template: Win a dink war by {{skill}} and {{when}}, then speed up when {{condition}}.

explanation.correct: Dink war: keep it low, vary placement to force movement, then speed up when they're vulnerable.
explanation.incorrect: Win the dink war with control, placement variety, and timing your speed-up for when they're tired or pop one up.
explanation.sayThisLine: Low dinks, varied placement, perfect timing on the speed-up.

payload.prompt: Match each soft-game concept from this unit.

pairs.definition: Slow, patient rallies of dinks and resets, waiting for an opponent to make a mistake.
Cross-court, straight, and angled dinks used to move opponents and create openings.
A soft, defensive shot that absorbs pace and lands in the kitchen to stay in the rally.

distractorDefinitions: A hard volley at the net

explanation.summary: Soft game is the foundation (dinking patience). Patterns are tactical (placement variety). Reset is defensive (absorbing pace).
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft game: patience. Patterns: tactics. Reset: defense.
